name: Levelorder Linewise Zig Zag
statement:
1. You are given a partially written GenericTree class.
2. You are required to complete the body of levelorderLineWiseZZ function. The function is expected to visit every node in "levelorder fashion" but in a zig-zag manner i.e. 1st level should be visited from left to right, 2nd level should be visited from right to left and so on. All nodes on same level should be separated by a space. Different levels should be on separate lines. Please check the question video for more details.
3. Input is managed for you.
outputFormat:
All nodes on the same level should be separated by a space.
1st level should be visited left to right, 2nd from right to left and so on alternately.
All levels on separate lines starting from top to bottom.

editorial:
The problem here deals with printing the tree in levels where every level should be printed in different lines as well as the direction of traversal should alternate within adjacent levels i.e. from left to right in level 1 to right to left in level 2 and so on.

Consider the following example:

The output for the given tree should be:

10

40 30 20

50 60 70 80 90 100

120 110

The problem here is an extension to our previous problem, Level Order Traversal Linewise. The idea here is to maintain two stacks one main stack which stores the nodes at the current level and another child stack which stores the elements of the next level. Here, as we need to alternate the direction of traversing a particular node, so for that we will have a variable, say level variable which will let us know at which level we are and whether we have to reverse the nodes at this particular level or not. Like in our previous problem, whenever our main stack gets empty we need to interchange the stacks and add a new line for the next level.

Now let's try to dry run the above-mentioned example,

Firstly we have mStack {10} and cStack {null} and level = 0

Now we remove 10 from mStack and print it then we will insert all its children in cStack (as level%2==0) from left to right

Now we have mStack {null} and cStack {40, 30, 20}

Hence interchanging stacks, mStack {40, 30, 20} and cStack {null}. Incrementing level, we have level = 1

The point here to note is that whenever our mStack becomes empty it implies that we have completed the current level completely and hence we need to move to the next level. This movement can be achieved only if we have a valid zig-zag order of nodes present of the next level somewhere, here comes our cStack, which if we observe then it already has stored the next level alternately from the above level, so all we need to do is to point our mStack to cStack and make our cStack empty. This ensures that we are already at the next level and now cStack will be storing the next level further down.

Continuing the dry run, Now we remove 40 from mStack and print it then we will insert all its children in cStack (as level%2!=0) from right to left

Now we have mStack {30, 20} and cStack {100}

Now we remove 30 from mStack and print it then we will insert all its children in cStack (as level%2!=0) from right to left

Now we have mStack {20} and cStack {70, 80, 90, 100}

Now we remove 20 from mStack and print it then we will insert all its children in cStack (as level%2!=0) from right to left

Now we have mStack {null} and cStack {50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100}

Hence interchanging stacks, mStack {50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100} and cStack {null}. Incrementing level, we have level = 2

Now we remove 50 from mStack and print it then we will insert all its children in cStack (as level%2==0) from left to right

Now we have mStack {60, 70, 80, 90, 100} and cStack {null}

Now we remove 60 from mStack and print it then we will insert all its children in cStack (as level%2==0) from left to right

Now we have mStack {70, 80, 90, 100} and cStack {null}

Now we remove 70 from mStack and print it then we will insert all its children in cStack (as level%2==0) from left to right

Now we have mStack {80, 90, 100} and cStack {null}

Now we remove 80 from mStack and print it then we will insert all its children in cStack (as level%2==0) from left to right

Now we have mStack {90, 100} and cStack {120, 110}

Now we remove 90 from mStack and print it then we will insert all its children in cStack (as level%2==0) from left to right

Now we have mStack {100} and cStack {120, 110}

Now we remove 100 from mStack and print it then we will insert all its children in cStack (as level%2==0) from left to right

Now we have mStack {null} and cStack {120, 110}

Hence interchanging stacks, mStack {120, 110} and cStack {null}. Incrementing level, we have level = 3

Now we remove 120 from mStack and print it then we will insert all its children in cStack (as level%2!=0) from right to left

Now we have mStack {110} and cStack {null}

Now we remove 110 from mStack and print it then we will insert all its children in cStack (as level%2!=0) from right to left

Now we have mStack {null} and cStack {null}

Hence our loop breaks and code ends.

Below is the implementation in Java:

public static void levelOrderLinewiseZZ(Node node) {
                                    Stack
 stack = new Stack<>();
                                    stack.add(node);
                                    Stack
 cstack = new Stack<>();
                                    int level = 0;
                                    while (stack.size() > 0) {
                                        node = stack.pop();
                                        System.out.print(node.data + " ");
                                        if (level % 2 == 0) {
                                            for (int i = 0; i < node.children.size(); i++) {
                                                Node child = node.children.get(i);
                                                cstack.push(child);
                                            }
                                        } else {
                                            for (int i = node.children.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
                                                Node child = node.children.get(i);
                                                cstack.push(child);
                                            }
                                        }
                                        if (stack.size() == 0) {
                                            stack = cstack;
                                            cstack = new Stack<>();
                                            level++;
                                            System.out.println();
                                        }
                                    }
                                }

Time Complexity: O(n)

The time complexity for the function is linear as we are traversing every node in the tree.

Space Complexity: O(n)

The space complexity for the function is linear as we are maintaining two stacks to store nodes.
